description: Seed registry of hypotheses, conventions and presets for closed-loop null-space exploration (epic #12593). Seeded by NSX-00 (#12549). Loader and CI citation gate land in NSX-11 (#12556).

schema_note.hypotheses: id, statement, parameters, source, verification_status. A hypothesis is a physiological or modelling prior that conditions a FAMILY_DEPENDENT output. statement is user-facing and must not rely on a source whose verification_status is UNVERIFIED or REMOVED.
schema_note.conventions: id, statement, parameters. A convention is a choice of metric, scale or frame; it is not physiology and never appears in an INVARIANT claim as a hypothesis.
schema_note.presets: id, label, hypotheses, conventions. A preset is a named hypothesis set for the UI; every id must exist.
schema_note.torque_capacity: Empty until NSX-04 (#12553). Each entry: joint_slot, direction, tau_max_nm, scaling_rule, population, source, verification_status, assumed (bool). An entry without a verified source must set assumed=true and verification_status=UNVERIFIED.
schema_note.source: Object {citation_id | null, note}. citation_id refers to citations[] below.
schema_note.verification_status: One of VERIFIED, UNVERIFIED, REMOVED, NOT_APPLICABLE (a modelling choice with no empirical claim).

citations.reference: Stanev D., Moustakas K. Modeling musculoskeletal kinematic and dynamic redundancy using null space projection. PLoS ONE 14(1):e0209171 (2019).
citations.claim_checked: Abstract: bounds on joint reaction loads from the feasible muscle-force space; misinterpretation is possible if null-space forces are ignored.

citations.reference: Choi H., Park S. Three Dimensional Upper Limb Joint Kinetics of a Golf Swing with Measured Internal Grip Force. Sensors 20(13):3672 (2020).
citations.claim_checked: Abstract: six-axis force-torque instrumented grip, nine professional golfers; right-hand torque about three times the left-hand torque.

citations.reference: Nesbit S.M., Serrano M. Work and Power Analysis of the Golf Swing. J Sports Sci Med 4(4):520-533 (2005).
citations.claim_checked: Bibliographic record, abstract and Table 3 swing efficiencies (20.2 to 26.8 percent); no two-thirds statement found.

hypotheses.statement: Each actuated joint can sustain a torque of at most its declared capacity in each direction; torques beyond capacity are excluded from the feasible set.

source.note: Capacities are a population prior; values and sources arrive with NSX-04.

hypotheses.statement: Among admissible allocations, the representative minimises the sum of squared torques each divided by its joint capacity.
The representative penalises the squared torque rate, favouring smooth torque histories.
Positive and negative joint power carry separate costs c_plus and c_minus; with c_plus equal to c_minus the cost reduces to a net-power term plus absolute power.

source.note: Modelling choice; identity proved in the specification.

hypotheses.statement: Each hand keeps at least a declared axial squeeze on the club, so hand contact never goes slack.

source.note: Preload magnitudes are not sourced here; Choi and Park 2020 measured internal grip forces but no value is adopted.

hypotheses.statement: Contact loads lie inside a friction cone with a declared coefficient, approximated by a polyhedron with a declared facet count and error bound.

conventions.statement: Closure rows and hand wrenches are expressed in the grip frame: origin at the midpoint of the two grip points, u along the shaft toward the clubhead, v the face-normal projection orthogonal to u, w = u x v.

parameters.sign: +J_c^T lambda acts on the tree; the closing hand exerts -lambda on the club

conventions.statement: Torque norms are weighted by inverse squared joint capacity.
Torque norms use the identity metric on actuated torques.
Torque norms use the inverse mass matrix on actuated coordinates; this is a labelled metric and is not Gauss's principle.
Forces are scaled by a characteristic force and moments by a characteristic moment before rank decisions and in null-space coordinates.
Numerical rank uses a relative singular-value tolerance against the largest singular value of the scaled matrix.
